title: Function output parse & latency profile at scale — KV cache + VPC considerations
summary: Deep technical session focusing on structured output (JSON mode) overheads when using function/tool calling at scale. We profiled constrained-decoding costs, KV cache hit/miss characteristics across cold and warm starts, batching tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem network and memory considerations. Agreed to run an additional microbenchmark (constrained-decode vs unconstrained JSON-safe parsing) and share raw latency histograms and config snippets.
topics: KV cache cold vs warm behavior
VPC/on-prem network egress and TLS overhead
Next steps: microbenchmarks and config recommendations
action_items: Priya Rao | Run constrained-decode microbenchmarks (json-mode vs unrestricted) and produce p50/p95/p99 CSV | 2026-04-21
Liam O'Connor | Share representative prompt+toolchain used in prod (including function schema examples) | 2026-04-16
Maya Singh | Provide KV cache access pattern traces (sampled) and cold start logs | 2026-04-18
Avery Chen | Share Redwood's internal perf harness and suggested runbook for on-prem sizing | 2026-04-20
next_steps: Schedule follow-up 1:1 to review p95 spikes and KV-miss remediation
Share security docs for VPC private deploys and HSM/KMS integration notes
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-14 16:00 UTC | Duration: 64m | Attendees: Avery Chen, Priya Rao (Redwood); Liam O'Connor, Maya Singh, Daniel Ruiz (Mosaic)

Summary: quick intro, then progressively deeper into constrained decoding overhead when returning structured JSON from a model via function calls. Lots of profiling numbers, some noisy transcription where acronyms appear, and a clear set of follow-ups.

00:00 - Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check, is the time good?
00:07 - Liam O'Connor: Yeah this works. morning here. thanks for taking time.
00:12 - Priya Rao: Cool. We'll go through the profile we ran on your toy workload, then look at KV cache behavior and batching. we also annotated the runs with the VPC-enabled latencies so you see network effects.
00:23 - Maya Singh: quick note, we run in a strict on prem env with V P C egress rules, and our functions call volume is pretty high, like 600 RPS at peak.
00:33 - Daniel Ruiz: also perimeter: we use HSM-backed K M S, and TLS termination is in the customer network. that might matter for handshake overheads.
00:40 - Avery Chen: good call. ok first slide: json-mode vs freeform. when you ask the model to output strict JSON (we call it json-mode / parse-safe mode), the decoder is constrained — and that adds CPU on the tokenization/validation path. the interesting bit is that the extra work is not linear; small payloads are cheap, but once you hit nested arrays with function args it grows.
00:58 - Liam O'Connor: can you give ballpark numbers? we saw p95 jump in our logs when we moved to structured payloads.
01:05 - Priya Rao: yes, in our microbench we saw about 6-12% added latency at p50 for simple json outputs, but p95 increased 20-35% depending on sequence length and the parser strictness. repeated function calls inside a single response (function chaining) compounds this because each tool call enforces schema validation.
01:24 - Maya Singh: when you say parser validation, is that on the agent side or inside the model runtime?
01:30 - Priya Rao: it's a mix. the constrained decoding is inside the model decoding loop — we restrict token choices to keep output JSON-safe — plus we run a post-emit validation/parsing stage. the post-stage does structural checks, and sometimes sanitization, e.g., closing braces, escape sequences. both stages add latency.
01:48 - Daniel Ruiz: So is the extra latency mostly CPU or memory bound? we care because our nodes are memory limited on prem.
01:54 - Priya Rao: mostly CPU + some memory for intermediate parse buffers. notably, quantized runtimes can shift costs — 4-bit quant tends to reduce token generation time, but the CPU parsing overhead remains similar; therefore the parsing can become the dominant fraction of end-to-end latency when you heavily quantize.
02:13 - Avery Chen: to add, when you quantize you reduce GPU time but leave more pressure on the host CPU for post-processing. we often see a break-even point where further quantization doesn't help overall p95.
02:25 - Liam O'Connor: ok that aligns with our hypothesis. what about KV cache? we saw inconsistent warmups.
02:32 - Priya Rao: yes KV cache hit quality matters a ton. we profiled cold start vs warm start. cold starts with a cold KV cache (misses on prefix keys) add a lot — roughly 30-60ms extra per request on our baseline for a 2k token window. warm hits reduced that substantially.
02:50 - Maya Singh: is that network bound in the V P C case? since our cache is persisted?
02:54 - Priya Rao: depends on placement. if KV is co-located on the same subnet/instance pool, latency is low. but in your V P C setup with cross-subnet routing and TLS to a managed store, you can see additional 10-40ms depending on egress and handshake reuse. in our VPC-onprem runs, we instrumented the TLS handshake reuse rate and found initial requests pay handshakes.
03:15 - Daniel Ruiz: we do keep connections alive but sometimes they recycle. are keepalive settings important?
03:19 - Priya Rao: yes keepalives and connection pooling are major levers. small tuning: increase pool size for hot threads, tune idle timeouts to avoid premature TLS teardown. we provided a suggested baseline in the repo.
03:31 - Liam O'Connor: about batching — our app is latency-sensitive. we want some batching for cost-savings but can't spike p95. what's Redwood's guidance?
03:40 - Avery Chen: tradeoff is clear. batching increases throughput and reduces per-token GPU cost, but increases queuing latency. with continuous batching, you can set max-wait thresholds and target p95 SLOs; recommend conservative batch windows (2-6ms) for low-latency apps. for very tight latency budgets you should prefer small batches and rely on prefix KV cache to amortize model work.
04:00 - Maya Singh: do you have numbers for the impact of 5ms vs 20ms batch windows?
04:05 - Priya Rao: in our throughput model with your token distribution, moving from 5ms to 20ms improved throughput ~2.6x but p95 latency grew by roughly the delta (15ms) plus queuing queers; overall p95 moved up by ~30-40ms because of longer tails. so if your SLO is 200ms p95, you can tune up. if you're aiming 100ms p95, keep small windows.
04:28 - Liam O'Connor: notable, thanks. another area: tool/function call overhead. we see extra hops when the model triggers a function and we execute a backend HTTP call. how much does Redwood add for the function/structured handing?
04:42 - Priya Rao: function invocation pattern: model emits a tool call, we serialize payload, call your service, await response, and then resume decoding. extra overhead is typically in (a) payload size roundtrip and (b) resuming decoder state. if you keep tool payloads small (IDs or small JSONs) the overhead is low; but when tool responses are large and re-injected as context (>=512 tokens), the resumed decode cost rises due to KV cache growth and attention matrix recompute.
05:08 - Daniel Ruiz: about resumed decode — does the runtime re-encode the tool result into token ids every time? is there caching for common tool outputs?
05:16 - Priya Rao: yes re-encoding happens. we do have prefix caching and can store common tool outputs as cached keys (if you opt in), which reduces recompute. but that requires determinism in tool outputs or a stable canonicalization to be effective.
05:30 - Avery Chen: there's also an opportunity: for on-prem customers we ship a small local cache service that persists canonical tool results to avoid repeated re-encode. but it needs config for TTLs and space.
05:41 - Liam O'Connor: curious about constrained decoding inside the model: can you disable schema enforcement at the decoder and do post-hoc repair to save latency?
05:50 - Priya Rao: yes, that's an engineering choice. we offer three modes: strict-decode (token masking to enforce schema), soft-decode (prefer schema but allow occasional off-schema tokens, then patch), and post-parse-only (no masking). strict-decode gives highest downstream correctness but costs more. soft-decode tends to be a good middle ground for many customers.
06:08 - Maya Singh: any empirical numbers for soft vs strict?
06:11 - Priya Rao: rough numbers from our runs: strict adds about 10-25% CPU parse overhead on p95; soft adds only ~5-10% because fewer masks; post-parse-only adds negligible decode overhead but post-processing p95 can spike due to repairs and retries — sometimes you endure an extra round-trip if repair triggers another generation.
06:31 - Daniel Ruiz: For on-prem, memory footprint with quantization: is 4-bit safe? we have small cards.
06:36 - Priya Rao: 4-bit quant is usable but watch out: some kernels use fused layers that increase peak working memory during attention recompute. also the runtime might temporarily allocate larger buffers during KV cache spills. rule of thumb: estimate 1.2-1.4x peak memory when enabling quantization versus the nominal static model size due to transient buffers.
06:56 - Avery Chen: also note that offloading strategies (CPU staging) add latency variability. if you're very latency-sensitive, avoid CPU-staging for hot paths.
07:05 - Liam O'Connor: network considerations again: do you recommend colocating KV store with model nodes in the V P C?
07:10 - Priya Rao: strongly yes. colocation reduces cross-subnet hops and TLS overhead. if your deployment cannot colocate, then ensure persistent TLS sessions and consider a local memcached/redis shim to reduce roundtrips.
07:22 - Maya Singh: how about guardrails for on-prem cert rotation? we saw some ephemeral timeouts around cert rotation windows.
07:28 - Priya Rao: set rolling cert rotation and increase prefetch window so active connections drain gracefully. also set probes to reestablish pooled connections preemptively during rotation to avoid thundering rehandshakes.
07:40 - Liam O'Connor: switching topic: do we need to change our function schema style to reduce tokens? we send verbose schemas.
07:47 - Priya Rao: yep smaller schemas = less overhead. you can choose compact naming and rely on enforced types in the decoder. also use short enumerations and map long human-friendly field descriptions out-of-band to the developer console.
08:00 - Daniel Ruiz: quick question about metrics: which counters should we capture to debug p95 spikes?
08:06 - Priya Rao: capture per-request: model decode time, parser validation time, function roundtrip time, kvcache hit/miss, batch delay, TLS handshake count, and quantization offload events. Redwood console surfaces most of these but please add application-level tagging to tie events to your request IDs.
08:22 - Maya Singh: thanks. we will.
08:25 - Avery Chen: ok let's walk through the microbench we ran — Priya, do you want to call out the config?
08:29 - Priya Rao: sure. Config notes: model: rdx-large-compat (open variant), sequence lengths sampled from your production distribution (mean 640 tokens, 95th 1800). quant: 8-bit and 4-bit variants tested. batch window: 0,5,20ms. KV store: local redis vs remote managed store (with a 10-40ms median). JSON mode: strict/soft/post-parse. Tool payloads: small (<=64 bytes) and large (~700 tokens). Key result: p95 is dominated by three things: resumed decode when tool responses are large, KV cache cold misses, and parser strictness in strict-mode. Other effects are additive.
09:04 - Liam O'Connor: can you share raw histograms?
09:07 - Avery Chen: we'll share. included in the repo is p50/p95/p99 CSVs and the underlying traces.
09:14 - Maya Singh: re: repo — is there sample code to integrate the local canonicalization cache you mentioned?
09:18 - Priya Rao: yes there's a small shim in the repo under examples/onprem-cache, and a README about TTL patterns. it's minimal but should be enough to test.
09:25 - Daniel Ruiz: any gotchas with the shim and concurrency?
09:28 - Priya Rao: make it single writer per key or use CAS to avoid partial canonicalizations. we documented a lightweight lock approach.
09:35 - Liam O'Connor: security: since we ar in health tech, we must avoid raw PHI in tool outputs. do you support redaction hooks?
09:42 - Priya Rao: yes, we have a server-side redaction hook and optional client-side filters. the server hook runs post-emit and can scrub tokens before they hit logs or downstream backends. the tradeoff is added latency — we measured ~10-30ms depending on regex complexity.
09:59 - Maya Singh: that could bite. can we run async redaction and delay logging instead?
10:03 - Priya Rao: yes you can opt to log only hashed digests and run async full redaction to keep SLOs intact. documented pattern in the security guide.
10:12 - Avery Chen: ok nearing wrap — let's summarize action items and owners.
10:16 - Avery Chen: Priya to run and share the constrained-decode microbenchmarks with p50/p95/p99 CSVs; Liam to share prod prompts and function schema samples; Maya to share KV traces and cold start logs; Avery to share perf harness and on-prem sizing notes.
10:30 - Liam O'Connor: sounds good. final quick question: any recommended short-term config to immediately reduce p95?
10:36 - Priya Rao: short-term: switch strict->soft decode, enable prefix KV caching for hot prefixes, lower batch windows to 5ms and use small tool payloads. that'll likely shave 20-60ms off p95 in our tests.
10:48 - Daniel Ruiz: thanks — we'll try that on staging.
10:51 - Avery Chen: Great. I'll send the repo link + perf CSVs and we'll set up the follow-up after you run the bench. thanks everyone.
10:58 - Maya Singh: thanks all. bye.

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "V P C" separated), truncations and filler. Linked artifacts mentioned: https://redwood.ai/perf/repo (shared), examples/onprem-cache README, security-guide/redaction-patterns.pdf.

End of transcript.
